learning_objective: 🎯 Apply trigonometric ratios to real-world scenarios to calculate the heights of tall structures and distances without actually measuring them physically!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: The imaginary straight line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer.
The angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the object is ABOVE the horizontal level (i.e., you have to raise your head to look at it).
The angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the object is BELOW the horizontal level (i.e., you have to lower your head to look at it).
Most problems require drawing a right-angled triangle, identifying the known angle and side, and using tan θ (Perpendicular/Base) to find the unknown height or distance.

fun_activity.title: 🌲 The Tree Height Hacker
fun_activity.instructions: Walk away from a tree until you can see its top at a 45° angle. Because tan(45°) = 1, your distance from the tree is exactly equal to the tree's height (plus your eye level height)!

exam_tips: 📌 Drawing a neat, labeled diagram carries marks. Even if your final calculation is wrong, a correct diagram will get you partial credit.
📌 The angle of depression from the top of a building to an object is equal to the angle of elevation from the object to the top of the building (Alternate Interior Angles).
📌 Always state clearly what 'x' or 'h' represents in your diagram (e.g., 'Let h be the height of the tower').
quick_recap: ⭐ The 'tan' ratio is the most frequently used trigonometric ratio in this chapter.
⭐ If the observer's height is given, subtract it from the total height before applying trigonometry to the triangle.
⭐ Theodolites are real instruments used by surveyors to measure these exact angles.
